summary:
Perak stands under Malaysia's national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of "gross indecency" with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, and these provisions are not limited to Malaysians. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Every Malaysian state, Perak included, maintains a Sharia enactment criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", carrying up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, while the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops at checks.

A crackdown has been underway since the 2018 election. Police raided a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur in October 2022 with at least 20 LGBT people arrested, an August 2022 raid on an LGBT venue produced twenty male arrests, a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned, and in November 2023 Johor announced plans for conversion-therapy centres.

Queue-and-venue raids carry the sharpest exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media had been pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid, the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions on 2 December, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional; the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Official hostility is explicit. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the national capital district's Islamic religious department (Jawi) had his full licence to carry out enforcement actions against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled abroad and received UNHCR protection.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months, and documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded, there is no same-sex marriage, and no federal law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. A 2022 Human Rights Watch report, drawing on interviews with 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021, documents state religious authorities harassing LGBT activists and organisations and raiding private events across the federation. The report names no Perak-specific enforcement case, and no Perak-specific evidence appears in the audited sources; the national framework governs visitor exposure here.
tangentialFactors:
Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported at national level, with transgender people identified as particularly vulnerable. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters published their report "I Don't Want to Change Myself — Anti-LGBT Conversion Practices, Discrimination, and Violence in Malaysia" on 10 August 2022, based on 73 interviews conducted across the country between 2018 and 2021.

Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had drawn at least 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and government-funded mukhayyam retreats sit alongside the conversion-therapy centres planned for Johor in November 2023.

Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, and LGBT events and media content are censored, so legislative change is unlikely during a visitor's stay.

The enforcement posture differs by venue rather than by province: the Caning sentence imposed on a lesbian couple by a Terengganu Sharia court shows that religious courts reach conduct as well as presentation, while the Kuala Lumpur sauna operation shows that venue raids generate the mass, public exposure of foreign nationals.
localsOnly:
Malaysia's Sharia cross-dressing offences apply to Muslim residents of Perak and are enforced by the state Islamic religious department; three states additionally bar women from posing as men, and the enactments never define what transgender dressing means, leaving enforcement to officer discretion.

Residents live under a dual court system in which the Sharia layer applies only to Muslims and the federal Penal Code applies to everyone, with no legal gender-recognition procedure available at either level.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination or hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no route to same-sex marriage or partner recognition.

State religious authorities have harassed LGBT activists and organisations and raided private events across the federation, and government-run rehabilitation programmes had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021.

Arrest records carry long-term consequences beyond release: detainees' images and personal details were leaked to media in the November 2025 operation, and 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended from their jobs.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Perak-specific enforcement case, arrest, or religious-department action appears in the audited sources; whether Perak's Sharia enactment also bars women from posing as men, as three states do, is not sourced here.

The audited sources do not establish whether the raid pattern documented in Kuala Lumpur in November 2025 and in Penang days later has any counterpart in Perak, or how often Perak's religious department exercises its caning and imprisonment powers.

The status of the constitutional challenge pending as of late 2014, filed after the mass arrest of 16 trans women on 8 June 2014, is not resolved in the sources, and the Federal Court's 2021 and 2024 judgments are reported on federalism grounds rather than on the substance of the cross-dressing offences.

The Human Dignity Trust profile is dated 16 December 2025 and the Human Rights Watch report fieldwork closes in 2021, so conditions after those dates are not independently sourced in this inventory.
